title: AI Built a Photoshop Clone in a Day. I Asked Experts What Happens Next
summary: Researchers explore implications of AI building a Photoshop clone in a day

Today, off-the-shelf models can spin up functional applications from scratch in a matter of hours—from niche multi-monitor utilities to sprawling, zero-cost clones of Adobe Photoshop and Microsoft Office.
But as the barrier to entry collapses, it leaves behind an urgent legal and ethical minefield: Is reverse-engineering industry-standard software legal?
Are these vibe-coded apps a genuine threat to professional developers, or just fragile, insecure knockoffs?
To separate hype from reality, I spoke with engineers, founders, and IP lawyers to understand what happens when anyone can clone any app.
A point of clarification: When I say AI apps, or vibe-coded apps, I’m talking about software generated by prompting an AI model or, at least, created with significant assistance from one.

It’s fairly common to call something vibe-coded when you actually think it’s slop (buggy, insecure, or otherwise poorly made by or with an AI model), but I use the term to differentiate between apps largely coded by humans and those coded by AI models.
Take Stagehand, a utility I vibe-coded with Opus 5.5 that makes managing a multi-monitor setup on Windows 11 easier.
I didn’t write any of the code; instead, I prompted an AI model, and it wrote the code for me.
Stagehand relies, in part, on Equalizer APO , a free, human-written utility that’s been around for well over a decade, long before AI models became accessible to consumers.
So, Stagehand is vibe-coded, while Equalizer APO isn’t.
Nonetheless, both apps work for me, regardless of the use of AI during their development.
Stagehand, of course, is just a small-scale example of what AI models can create.
ArtCraft, the aforementioned suite that includes clones of popular creativity and productivity apps, is a different matter entirely.
Those apps aren't just infinitely more complex—they also pose some thorny questions for traditional software companies and developers.

To get some background and perspective on the project, I spoke with ArtCraft's founder and CEO, Brandon Thomas, about the AI-assisted development process for PhotoCraft (ArtCraft’s open-source Photoshop competitor) and more.
Although Thomas is a seasoned software development professional who knows how to code, he developed the first version of PhotoCraft by prompting an AI model.
He explains, “I laid out how it was to be architected.
I planned out that the UI components need to live in a different place than all of the functional components, all of the file format reading, and all of that.

That all of these things need to be independently tested and vetted.” He allowed the AI to look at screenshots of Photoshop’s interface and to rely on its preexisting understanding of how the app works, but forbade it from accessing bytecode, source code, or the underlying application itself.
Thomas spent about 24 hours creating the first version.
This kind of workflow isn’t the norm for software development in 2026, even if AI tools continue to proliferate.
No governing body certifies apps as vibe-coded or not, so the functional distinction between something like PhotoCraft and Photopea is ultimately somewhat flimsy.
Does the use of AI in an app's development really matter to you if it works well?
I’m many things—a gamer, a journalist, and one of those self-important people who describes himself as a foodie—but I’m not a heavy user of Adobe's creative software.
Luckily, here at PCMag, we have experts who are, such as our resident camera specialist, Jim Fisher .
Fisher used PhotoCraft (alongside LightCraft, ArtCraft's take on Adobe Lightroom ) and came away largely impressed by its performance.

He wrote, “I'm pleasantly surprised by just how close ArtCraft's LightCraft and PhotoCraft recreate their Adobe counterparts.” However, that’s not to say these apps can do everything as well as Adobe; Fisher calls out minor complaints such as the lack of Camera Matching color profiles, a less advanced noise reduction engine, and slightly less fine detail in rendered images, among other things.
It’s hard not to be blown away by the fact that a free application like PhotoCraft, which took only a day to get the first working version, can legitimately compete with Photoshop.
This is doubly true because their practically identical interfaces mean switching requires almost no workflow adjustments.
Some ArtCraft apps are less competitive with the apps they emulate, however, and it isn’t shy about pointing out those gaps.
Take, for example, WordCraft, ArtCraft’s take on Microsoft Word.
Based on the official parity assessment , WordCraft is only roughly 60% ready for real work at the time of writing, which probably won’t tempt too many people to switch over from Word.
That said, the first version of Microsoft Word was launched in 1983, more than four decades ago, while the first commit to WordCraft’s GitHub occurred on October 6, 2026.

Thomas is optimistic, if not outright bullish, about achieving parity: “I do not see anything in the world of software engineering that these [AI] models will not be able to do.” He continued, “I think small teams of people or even individuals will be able to build anything they imagine.”
Parity aside, good software is more than just the features it supports.

Otherwise, if a user finds a bug, what happens?”
I brought this idea to Thomas, and he wasn’t fazed, telling me that ArtCraft has a Discord community that’s grown so rapidly that a representative reached out to assign him an official support contact.
And this isn’t just a community of users, either.
ArtCraft started with Thomas, but it’s grown much bigger than him, becoming a collective development effort similar to Linux.
According to Thomas, a core team of around 30 contributors is already working on Craft apps alongside him, while thousands of developers collaborate with them.
The answer to Vignoli’s question of what happens when a bug gets discovered is simple: In ArtCraft’s case, the community built a Discord bot for filing bug reports.
Photopea’s Kutskir isn’t worried about developers like ArtCraft or apps like PhotoCraft replacing him just yet.

“Even if I try to learn everything and make the ultimate app…and make it in a month, that doesn’t mean I’ll be able to attract the users from other apps.”
Though an app like PhotoCraft is impressive, it’s hard not to see Kutskir’s logic.
If you’re already happy with Photopea (or any other photo editor), is there really much practical reason to swap over to PhotoCraft, especially given how new it is?
Whether to swap over to an app like PhotoCraft is more than an existential question; it’s also a practical one.
AI apps can be more private and respectful of your data, considering they often don’t require sending your data to a corporation’s servers, but reliability and security issues are still commonplace.
For example, I’ve vibe-coded three feature-complete apps that do exactly what I want them to, as well as a handful of mods.
Each time, bugs and unintended interactions popped up that I had to squash.
I’m not a programmer, though, so I can only catch these by using my apps or if an AI model’s test suite catches them.
But even if you're a programmer overseeing an AI model, manually reviewing every single line of code it outputs is often unrealistic and would otherwise seriously undercut the tool's benefits.

If you take the pulse of online communities’ feelings on the reliability of AI apps , you quickly get the sense that vibe-coding produces only slop that barely works at best and is inevitably filled with bad design decisions and inefficiencies.
To some extent, I’ve seen developers express similar concerns, albeit not as strongly and phrased differently.
For Vignoli, this is a measure of the depth and reliability of LibreOffice’s features that AI-generated competitors may struggle to match.
For reference, WordCraft's current alpha build spans 88,000 lines of code, including documented bugs and issues.

When I brought these concerns to Thomas, he joked about having a grudge against LibreOffice (or maybe it was OpenOffice, LibreOffice’s predecessor, Thomas mused) for losing a paper he was writing back in college, which is an experience that underpins his actual point.
“I’ve had files get corrupted because the software was poorly coded.
It’s definitely been a thing that I’ve been frustrated at.

This is what maintaining an online service is like, and the [AI] models and tools that we build will help us [deal with bugs].”
Thomas sees bugs as an inevitable part of any software, but he sees AI as uniquely well-equipped to address this problem, especially as AI models become more advanced.
“Software is going to be more reliable, not less reliable,” he argues.
I’ve used Windows since long before AI went mainstream, so I definitely don’t have any illusions that 100% human-written software is uniquely resistant to bugs.
Accordingly, I’m at least open to the possibility that an always-on machine, overseen by a developer, might be able to churn through bugs more effectively.
